newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone mining firm denies troops seize Koidu.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone mining firm denies troops seize Koidu.

text.p: Police and community leaders in Sierra Leone's eastern town of Koidu said on Thursday soldiers had seized foreign-owned diamond mines there following Sunday's army coup, but a U.K. mining company there denied the report.
Michael Grunberg, a director of London-based Branch Energy Ltd, owned by DiamondWorks Ltd, said the town was calm.

"The Koidu area is peaceful and quiet and the relationship between the military and DiamondWorks is good. There is no aggressive action by the military. All commercial diamond activities have ceased but some artisanal mining is continuing," he said by telephone.

DiamondWorks is linked to Executive Outcomes, a South African company staffed by many former soldiers of the apartheid era which was hired by Sierra Leone's former military government in 1995 to ensure security in mining areas.
The DiamondWorks compound is guarded by armed security guards provided by a company called Lifeguard Management, set up jointly by Sierra Leoneans and Executive Outcomes.
But DiamondWorks insists that it and Branch Energy have no corporate links with Executive Outcomes, which has sometimes attracted negative publicity.
Grunberg said the DiamondWorks compound was sheltering about 100 Lebanese and around 30 other expatriates. "We have very cordial relations with the military," he said.
Canadian, British and Belgian mine operators are among hundreds of foreigners who have taken refuge at beachside hotels in Freetown hoping to join evacuation flights.
Low-ranking soldiers ousted civilian president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah on Sunday.

Diamonds are Sierra Leone's main export and foreign investors had hoped that the election of a civilian government in March 1996, and a peace accord signed with rebels of the Revolutionary United Front last November would improve the security situation.

In Massingbi, 50 km from Koidu, soldiers on Wednesday shot dead at least 20 members of a civilian militia loyal to Kabbah who had been stationed in the town before the coup to protect against rebel attacks, police in the regional capital Makeni said.

One of the first acts of the new Armed Forces Revolutionary Council was to ban the Kamajors, on whom Kabbah had come to rely against the rebels. They have refused to disband and have clashed with soldiers in several towns.
Community leaders in the area said Kamajors were gathering in Massingbi vowing revenge for Wednesday's killings. They feared an escalation of the violence.
